title: Finite convex certificates for quadratic informational substitutes
narration: When does more information bring diminishing returns? An Evidence Press audio briefing. Imagine predicting one numerical outcome using two reports. Each report has finitely many possible values, and prediction errors are measured by their squares. You may reveal only part of the first report, using fresh randomness. The question is whether the second report is always at least as valuable after this partial disclosure as it is after the first report has been revealed completely. There are infinitely many possible disclosure rules. This research candidate replaces that infinite test with finitely many mathematical checks. For each distinct average prediction from the first report, an auxiliary list of numbers must meet all the relevant squared-distance limits at once. These are convex feasibility problems. The result allows impossible combinations of reports; it does not assume that every combination occurs. When every combination is possible, the checks simplify to explicit comparisons between pairs of report values. But that shortcut has limits. One example with impossible combinations passes every two-state restriction and still fails when three states are mixed. Another example shows that pairwise checks can fail for a prediction with several numerical components, even when every report combination is possible. The practical use is screening an exactly specified information model, not proving that a real forecasting market will improve. Checking both disclosure directions requires applying the criterion twice. The work concerns two finite signals, one numerical target, and squared-error prediction. It does not cover arbitrary scoring rules or arbitrary pairs of partial disclosures. Written mathematical proofs support the general claims. Exact arithmetic checks support particular examples and certificates; they are not formal verification, and a numerical solver's approval is not automatically an exact certificate. This is an AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate. Internal assessments are provisional, not external peer review or a guarantee of novelty. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
oneLine: A finite convex criterion decides a specified diminishing-returns property for two finite signals and a scalar quadratic prediction target, including impossible signal combinations.
abstract: This unrefereed candidate characterises quadratic informational substitution for a scalar square-integrable target and two finite signals with arbitrary joint support. At each distinct source mean, one auxiliary completion vector must satisfy a weighted squared-distance budget for every source state. Compact minimax duality and scalar interpolation establish equivalence with every admissible randomised disclosure. The sharp residual-variance coefficient is an attained convex-program value when finite; full support reduces it to explicit directed pairwise ratios. Sparse scalar examples have exact coefficients 4/9 and 16/9. A full-support vector counterexample shows that pairwise sufficiency does not extend automatically to multicategory quadratic scoring.
citeText: Anonymous (2026). Finite convex certificates for quadratic informational substitutes. Version 0.1.0-candidate. Evidence Press. 10.5281/zenodo.23401650.
keyResults: Finite scalar-knot completion feasibility is necessary and sufficient for the universal disclosure inequality with arbitrary finite signal support.
The sharp residual-variance coefficient is an attained convex-program value whenever finite; equal-mean compatibility characterises finiteness.
Full rectangular support forces the completions and yields an explicit directed-pair formula and sharp normalised gap, not a minimum absolute disclosure gap.
Sparse scalar examples distinguish coefficients 4/9 and 16/9; in one orientation every two-state posterior restriction of A can pass while a three-state posterior fails.
A full-support vector example defeats pairwise sufficiency and admits a strictly positive four-category Brier realisation.
